items.text: Raw Materials: Studio Lenca - A Place Within Me For Salvadoran artist Studio Lenca – aka José Campos – El Salvador exists somewhere between memory and imagination. A place carried across distance, remembered through gestures and landscapes, and through the feeling of a home that was never entirely his to inhabit. Raised in the U.S., where his family lived as ‘illegal aliens’ after their displacement during the Salvadoran Civil War, Campos now uses his practice to reclaim autonomy over a fragmented history, merging biographical anecdotes, personal reflections, and folkloric iconography that unpack his own sense of belonging. - Meme Flores Returning to El Salvador in 2025 while developing work for his exhibition COSITAS, Campos connects with filmmaker and cinematographer Meme Flores to document his journey for the short film Studio Lenca - A Place Within Me . Shot on 16mm film between Castillo Venturoso and Campos’ hometown of Santiago Nonualco, the film grew through encounters with the landscapes, people and traditions that inform his relationship with El Salvador, from the Historiantes – traditional dancers who serve as a key reference in his art – to the distinct colors, sounds, and light that shape the environment. Finding a space where the familiar becomes slightly strange, Flores molds a quiet observation of the place we carry long after we have left it, stepping into Campos’ vision of El Salvador as somewhere held between closeness and distance.
items.title: Raw Materials: Studio Lenca - A Place Within Me

Evolving a hobby and vast personal collection into a 50-year career growing and shaping miniature trees, Graviano spent time working with legendary bonsai expert Frank Okamura while volunteering at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden before founding the Bonsai of Brooklyn in 1976 – one of the oldest businesses in the U.S. dedicated to the Japanese bonsai tradition. - Tony Blahd & Lydia Fine Now in his eighties, Graviano reflects on the landscape of memory, and a life deeply influenced by plants for the short documentary Picture a Tree , directed by Tony Blahd and Lydia Fine. First connecting in 2017 while sourcing bonsai trees for another project, Blahd found himself in Graviano's office, where soil-dusted carpets, and walls hung with bonsai tools and ephemera, compete with a miniature train set – complete with a massive scale model of his Brooklyn neighborhood – that occupies the basement. Returning to capture his world, and the patience and dedication demanded from bonsai cultivation, Picture a Tree weaves new interviews and archive footage into an exploration of the ways plants relate to creativity, philosophy, and ways of living, building a spirited ode to botanical obsession and Graviano’s quiet fascination with life in miniature.
items.title: ​Grounded: Picture a Tree

items.text: ​In Motion: The Rehearsal A sensual meditation on the ritual of rehearsal, and the creative rhythms between choreographer and performer, London-based choreographer Holly Blakey and director Fiona Jane Burgess construct a portrait of an artist and her process for the short film The Rehearsal . Created with biannual literary and art journal Erotic Review – exploring desire in its many forms – the black and white movement film speaks to the primal instinct that emerges through Blakey’s work, engaging with themes of eroticism, taboo, the grotesque, fragility, and beauty. - Fiona Jane Burgess Playing with the physical forms and archetypes of 20th century erotic photography, The Rehearsal honors the innate eroticism of dance, artistic collaboration and possibility, featuring movement artists Lewis Walker, Eve Stainton, and Sharia Johnson, alongside a close cast of dancers and Blakey’s frequent collaborators. Framing the rehearsal space as a place for freedom and failure, Burgess captures the dialogue that connects the choreographer to those who inhabit and inspire her work – centering the trust and closeness that defines the unspoken contract exchanged off-stage.

items.text: Raw Materials: Diego Delgado-Elias Drawn to historic buildings and the traces they carry, Peruvian designer and architect Diego Delgado-Elias has spent his 20-year career reinforcing the elements that develop a space’s warmth and character. Based in Paris, his architecture and interior design studio expands this affinity for creating lived-in spaces that seem to have accumulated naturally over time, observing the lives that occupied a house before him – left as marks on walls, layers of paint, or objects that appear frozen and unmoved. - Daniel Guix While working to restore a seventeenth-century house in the Provençal village of Visan, France, Delgado-Elias found a place that quietly mirrors his sentimental understanding and way of looking at spaces. Moving between past and present, the house becomes an echo of other spaces and sensations that remain with him, while bearing the influence of the surrounding nature in its preserved frescoes, original materials, and domestic objects. For a new short documentary, director Daniel Guix studies Delgado-Elias’ world through the house, exploring how our earliest encounters with spaces can mold our sensibility. Shooting on 16mm, to capture the grain, movement and texture of memory, Guix brings Delgado-Elias’ reflections into conversation with the house, as a rhythm that connects one room to the next, and a reminder of the formative impressions that unconsciously shape creative vision.
items.title: Raw Materials: Diego Delgado-Elias

items.text: Private View: ​Stefan Brüggemann: In No Time Based between London, Mexico City and Ibiza, Mexican conceptual artist Stefan Brüggemann unpacks the philosophy of language in text-driven works that carry acerbic or timely messages. Embedding social criticism in dynamic spray-painted or gold-leafed canvases, neon lights, and large-scale installations, Brüggemann’s work exists at the intersection of punk and refinement, intentionally disrupting the grandeur projected by his raw materials. Directed by Giacomo Gex and voiced by Iggy Pop, the short documentary Stefan Brüggemann: In No Time captures the artist through the faith and philosophy that drives him creatively, in a poetic reflection on the passing of time. - Stefan Brüggemann In Ibiza, Brüggemann’s studio-cum-residence has become a space for inspiration and recalibration, grounded in the island’s contrasts – reinforcing the artistic juxtapositions that sustain his practice. Staging interventions that inhabit the architecture and the surrounding environment, the film frames Stefan’s house and garden as a living artwork, with the island itself as a key character – shot between 16mm film, 8mm film, MiniDV tape and digital formats to document the calm and chaos of the landscape, and its distinctive color palette across the seasons.

items.text: Inner Worlds: Philippine Leroy-Beaulieu An icon of French cinema, best known internationally for her portrayal of the formidable Sylvie Grateau on Netflix’s global hit Emily in Paris , French actress Philippine Leroy-Beaulieu shares philosophical and intimate reflections at the greenhouse of Paris’ Jardin des Plantes, France’s principal botanical garden. Raised in Rome among her parents’ artist friends, Leroy-Beaulieu learned early on to seek out beauty and freedom. “I struggle with a world that's too rigid and standardized,” she says. “For me, life is something much more...undulating.” This year, Philippine Leroy-Beaulieu is the artistic director of the Oh La La! initiative at Art Basel Paris, a two-day rehang allowing galleries to transform their booths with new and thought-provoking works. Following the theme Myths and Legends, 45 galleries will participate and present artworks by Nina Childress, Leonora Carrington, Ed Ruscha, Diedrick Brackens, among others.Reflecting on her relationship with creativity, Leroy-Beaulieu says she is struck by artists’ unique approach to experience. “Rather than asserting things in an overly human way,” she explains, “they succeed in putting themselves in a position of ecstasy before something unknown that transcends us.” Drawn to the order within the seeming chaos of nature, and what humans cannot see but can feel, the actress follows her intuitions and flashes of insight. “The other world, the invisible world, catches my attention all the time,” she says. “I know it exists; I don't even need proof.”

items.text: ​Meet the artists by Art Basel: Ladji Diaby Carried by the magic and histories he finds in everyday objects, French-Malian artist Ladji Diaby creates works that tell stories that are at once personal and collective. A graduate of Beaux-Arts de Paris, the young artist staged his first institutional solo exhibition at Kunstverein Nürnberg in Germany in 2024, later marking his arrival on the international scene with his 2026 installation, ‘Who’s Gonna Save The World ?’ at Lafayette Anticipations in Paris. Presenting contemporary creatives shaping today’s cultural landscape, this episode of Art Basel’s Meet the artists series opens the door to Diaby’s studio in Ivry-sur-Seine – the Paris suburb where he grew up and still lives, and shares his artistic process. “As an artist, I see my gestures as tilling a soil made of memory,” he says. “I imagine my mind as land that I cultivate, where things gradually rise to the surface.” - Ladji Diaby At the Caverne des Particuliers, a local second-hand furniture store where Diaby once accompanied his mother on her shopping sprees, the abundance of materials and their spiritual resonance continue to inspire him. “Constraints become choices,” he says, “and you build an entire narrative around them: a political and artistic dialectic”. Here, repurposed objects, found on the street or sourced second-hand, are transformed into one-off talismans – echoing his mother’s habit of decorating and embellishing furniture to forge acloseness to God – reframing household items as quiet mechanisms of self-liberation. Ladji Diaby is represented by Galerie Crèvecoeur (Paris).

items.text: ICP’s Incubator is located on ICP’s ground floor. The space is free and open to the public during café and museum hours. Since 2018, photographer Melissa Ann Pinney has documented Chicago Public School students as part of an artist residency. As the students began to invite her into their world, the project became a document of identity, community and urgent social issues. Pinney’s thoughtful portraits of young people navigating the transformations of adolescence contain all of the triumph, grief, humor, and tenderness of growing up. About The ArtistMelissa Ann Pinney’s work first garnered attention in the Museum of Modern Art’s major 1991 exhibition, Pleasures and Terrors of Domestic Comfort. Her studies of the social lives and emerging identities of American adolescents have earned her many awards, including a Guggenheim Fellowship, three Illinois Arts Council Fellowship Awards, and a National Endowment for the Arts Midwest Regional Fellowship. Pinney was selected for three documentary projects that were exhibited, published, and archived in Chicago: Changing Chicago (1987), City 2000, and most recently, her work in the Chicago Public Schools. Pinney’s first monograph, Regarding Emma: Photographs of American Women and Girls (2003) was followed by Girl Ascending (2010), TWO (2015), and In Their Own Light: Photographs from Chicago Public Schools (2023).Recent exhibitions include The Outwin 2022: American Portraiture Today, at the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery, Go Down Moses at the Museum of Contemporary Photography Chicago (2019), A History of Photography, at the George Eastman Museum (2019 and 2023), Girl Transcendent at the Schneider International Gallery, Maui (2018), Photographs from the Collection, at the Art Institute of Chicago (2018), American Photographs, 1845 to Now, at the Amon Carter Museum of American Art (2017); The Gender Show, at the Fundación Canal, Madrid, Spain (2016), and Girls on the Verge: Portraits of Adolescence at the Art Institute of Chicago, 2008.Pinney’s photographs are in the collections of the Art Institute of Chicago, George Eastman Museum, J. Paul Getty Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, Museum of Fine Arts Houston, Museum of Modern Art, International Center of Photography, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and Whitney Museum of American Art, among others. About the ICP Incubator SpaceICP’s Incubator Space is a new exhibition program designed to highlight the work of emerging photographers who are responding in real time to the world around us. ICP will present a rotating selection of projects by imagemakers experimenting with and pushing boundaries around the documentary tradition. ICP’s Incubator Space is curated by Sara Ickow, Associate Director of Exhibitions at ICP.

items.text: In On Rape and Institutional Failure, an exhibition centered on the second chapter of her ongoing project A History of Misogyny, Laia Abril examines different forms of violence against women throughout history.Weaving together images, compiled testimonies, archival materials, select objects, and installations with sound and video, the exhibition investigates how gender-based stereotypes, coupled with worldwide prejudices and misconceptions, have contributed to a systemic rape culture that persists today. By focusing on institutions, Abril aims to avoid narratives of victim-blaming, instead addressing the on-going problem of social accountability that has allowed offenders and enablers alike to avoid justice. On Rape and Institutional Failure was first exhibited in 2020 in the wake of the initial, galvanizing allegations against Harvey Weinstein and other powerful men. While #MeToo has led to few sustained consequences and little systemic change, Abril offers a meaningful opportunity to address the long history of silencing victims and the transgenerational trauma that has developed as a result. Please Note: If you are feeling distressed as you move through Laia Abril: On Rape and Institutional Failure, please use the link here for resources and hotlines. https://uniqode.io/J4pZk3 About Laia Abril:Laia Abril (b. 1986) is a research-based artist working across photography, text, video, and sound, focusing on biopolitics and gender issues. Her work is rooted in a politically engaged, process-driven methodology that employs strategies of forensic aesthetics and counter-narratives, interrogating dominant histories and the politics of representation.Her work has been exhibited in over 25 countries and is held in collections such as Centre Pompidou, Photo Elysée, Fotomuseum Winterthur, MACBA, Reina Sofía, MNAC, and the V&A Museum. She has authored acclaimed books, including The Epilogue, Lobismuller, and the A History of Misogyny series: On Abortion, On Rape, and On Mass Hysteria.She has received the Foam Paul Huf Award (Amsterdam), RPS Hood Medal (London), Aperture Best Book Award (NY/Paris), and Spain’s National Photography Award. Based in Switzerland, she is a senior lecturer at HSLU and is represented by Les Filles du Calvaire in Paris and Set Espai d’Art in Spain. About Curator:Sara Ickow is the Associate Director of Exhibitions at the International Center of Photography, where she has been a curator on exhibitions including Gillian Laub: Family Matters, ICP at 50: From the Collection 1845–2019, To Conjure: New Archives in Recent Photography, and Photobooks USA 2000–25. She is also the Managing Director for Women Photograph and co-editor of the book Women Photograph: What We See. Previously, she worked as Curatorial Assistant and Collections Manager at the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery. Sara holds an MA in Art History from NYU’s Institute of Fine Arts. items.text: I’m So Happy You Are Here: Japanese Women Photographers from the 1950s to Now reconsiders and expands on the history of Japanese photography through the work twenty-eight intergenerational artists from the 1950s to today. Presented in partnership with Aperture and curated by Pauline Vermare, Lesley A. Martin, and Takeuchi Mariko, the exhibition includes work by Fujioka Aya, Hara Mikiko, Hiromix, Ishikawa Mao, Ishiuchi Miyako, Katayama Mari, Kawauchi Rinko, Komatsu Hiroko, Kon Michiko, Nagashima Yurie, Narahashi Asako, Ninagawa Mika, Nishimura Tamiko, Noguchi Rika, Nomura Sakiko, Okabe Momo, Okanoue Toshiko, Onodera Yuki, Sawada Tomoko, Shiga Lieko, Sugiura Kunié, Suzuki Nozomi, Tawada Yuki, Tokiwa Toyoko, Ushioda Tokuko, Watanabe Hitomi, Yamazawa Eiko and Yanagi Miwa.Spanning photography, installation, photobooks, and printed matter, the exhibition explores the experiences and perspectives of women in Japan through delicate and blunt observations of everyday life, critical reflections on the roles inhabited and reshaped by Japanese women, and approaches that push the boundaries of photography. The exhibition is accompanied by a major publication (Aperture, 2024) that expands upon content of the show through essays, historical material, and a comprehensive bibliography of photobooks made by Japanese women.I'm So Happy You Are Here is an exhibition with a strong international pedigree. Following its debut at Rencontres d’Arles, France (2024), the exhibition has traveled to The Hague (2024), Frankfurt (2025), London (2026), and Tokyo (2026), before arriving at ICP for its first US showing here in New York.Financial Times | Arles: “The highlight” of Rencontres d’Arles.W Magazine | London: “The Japanese Women Who Rewrote Photography’s Rules.”Time Out Tokyo | Tokyo: “The exhibition offers a vital counter-narrative to a photographic canon long dominated by male figures.” About Curators:Lesley A. Martin is executive director of Printed Matter. Most recently, she was the creative director of Aperture, where she served as editor on more than one hundred books on photography, and as founding publisher of The PhotoBook Review. Takeuchi Mariko is a photography critic, curator, and professor at Kyoto University of the Arts. Previously, she served as visiting researcher at the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo, and at the National Museum of Art, Osaka. Pauline Vermare is the Phillip and Edith Leonian Curator, Photography, Brooklyn Museum. Previously, she served as the cultural director of Magnum Photos in New York, and curator at the International Center of Photography and the Museum of Modern Art, New York. About Aperture:Aperture is a nonprofit publisher that leads conversations around photography worldwide. From its new home opening this September in New York, Aperture connects global audiences and supports artists through its acclaimed quarterly magazine, books, exhibitions, digital platforms, public programs, limited-edition prints, and awards. Established in 1952 to advance “creative thinking, significantly expressed in words and photographs,” Aperture champions photography’s vital role in nurturing curiosity and encouraging a more just, tolerant society. For more information, visit aperture.org Header image: Kawauchi Rinko, Untitled, 2004; from the series the eyes, the ears. Courtesy the artist and Aperture

items.text: Shooting without a cable has been possible in Capture One for years. What was missing was speed, and with it, the confidence to use wireless when the shoot depends on it. Wireless was the option you took when a cable wasn’t practical, not one you chose on merit. 2nd Gen Wireless Tethering was built to change that. Here’s how it works, why it works the way it does, and how to get the best results. The problem It’s tempting to treat slow wireless tethering as a software problem. The obvious responses are to optimize the transfer, tune the protocol, cut overhead. Those things help at the margins, but they don’t change the basic situation: the file still must cross the air. A full-resolution RAW file is tens of megabytes. A wireless connection on set rarely performs as well as its specification suggests. Other devices compete for the same network, other networks sit nearby, and the camera is writing to its own memory card at the same time. items.text: No flash, no studio. Here’s how three Capture One RAW Talent winners made their work and shared something true to themselves. Three winning projects. One is a set of portraits built around a single uncomfortable question. One is about the draft of air that moves through a subway passage. One is about people who live on boats. On paper they share nothing. In practice, none of the three used a flash. All three found their subject somewhere they had already walked past a hundred times.
